Google refuses a required or named tool choice for gpt-oss-120b, which calls one tool in a turn and sometimes answers outside the schema, and gpt-oss-120b and GLM-5.2 stop at a stop sequence in their reasoning.

# The Last Light

Elena had kept the light at Pinnacle Point for thirty-seven years. Every evening at dusk, she climbed the spiral staircase—ninety-two steps, she knew by heart—and lit the great lens that swept its beam across the dark Atlantic.

The work had changed around her. When she started, she kept logs by candlelight and listened to the radio for storms. Now a digital system monitored the tide, the wind, the fog, and could light the lamp without her. But she still came every evening, because the sea demanded respect, and machines didn't understand respect.

One November night, a fishing boat appeared on the horizon, tossing violently in fifty-knot winds. Elena watched it through binoculars, her stomach tightening. The automated systems said the light was functioning. But the boat was heading toward the shoals, and she could see the captain wasn't course-correcting.

She grabbed the auxiliary flare kit and climbed to the gallery. The wind nearly tore the door from her hands. She fired three flares into the black sky, each one bleeding red light across the clouds.

The boat changed course. Just barely, just in time.

Elena later learned the boat's navigation system had failed. The captain had been steering blind, looking for Pinnacle Point's beam but unable to distinguish it from the glow of town lights that had crept northward over the years.

That spring, the coast guard informed her the lighthouse would be decommissioned. They didn't need her anymore, they said. The light wasn't necessary.

Elena packed her things slowly. On her final night, she climbed the stairs one last time and lit the lamp manually, the old way. She stood in the warmth of its turning beam and listened to the waves.

Somewhere out there, someone might still be looking for the light.

He lit the lamp as dusk bled into the sea. The beam swung out, a slow, faithful arc. Ships would see it and steer clear. That was the promise.
